proposed_edges.relationship: Popper, Lakatos and the historian L. Pearce Williams criticise Kuhn's normal science and theory change: indoctrination, irrationalism, "mob psychology" and too little history (1965–70), answered by Kuhn
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read in Lakatos and Musgrave, eds., Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970; the 1965 Bedford College symposium). Popper, already a critic on the science roster: the normal scientist "has been taught in a dogmatic spirit: he is a victim of indoctrination" (p. 53); "Kuhn's logic is the logic of historical relativism" (p. 55); the Myth of the Framework "is, in our time, the central bulwark of irrationalism" (p. 56); yet "'Normal' science, in Kuhn's sense, exists" (p. 52). Lakatos, a contributor on the science roster: Kuhn's message "had some authoritarian and irrationalist overtones" (p. 92 n. 3); "in Kuhn's view scientific revolution is irrational, a matter for mob psychology" (p. 178, italicised in the original); he also absorbs Kuhn, offering his research programmes as a reconstruction of Kuhn's "socio-psychological concept of 'paradigm'" (p. 179 n. 1). L. Pearce Williams, a historian of science, aims at Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time. We simply do not know enough to permit a philosophical structure to be erected on a historical foundation"; "As a historian, then, I must view both Popper and Kuhn with a somewhat jaundiced eye" (p. 50), while continuing to use both as guides. Kuhn's replies: charges of "irrationality, relativism, and the defence of mob rule" are "labels which I categorically reject" (p. 234); such misinterpretations "are voiced only by philosophers" (p. 260); to Pearce Williams, "There is no area in which I am more deeply conscious of the need for additional historical research, though I dissent from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws from that need" (pp. 251–252); and in the 1970 Postscript, good reasons "function as values" (p. 199) and "That is not a relativist's position" (p. 206). The irrationalism charge came from philosophers on the science roster; the historian's objection was evidential. edge_332 (science → kuhn, influence) stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The target is a person entry. On the source side the arrow corresponds to the science strand normal_science_debates (Kuhn, Popper, Lakatos).

proposed_edges.relationship: Latour and Callon: the strong programme's symmetry is itself asymmetrical, explaining nature by society, so SSK must take "one more turn" (1992–99), after an acknowledged debt
proposed_edges.map_label: The strong programme as an obstacle, 1992–99
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Latour's own words, read. Debt first: in 1988 he wrote that Bloor "has most clearly defined the task of any sociology of science by introducing the notion of symmetry" and that "the principle of symmetry remains the basis of most work in the area", while dropping social explanation (Pasteurization of France, p. 256 n. 21); in 1999, "I feel entirely in David's debt" (p. 114); edge_685 records that debt. Critique: "One More Turn after the Social Turn" (1992; author's typescript, §2): "Bloor's book (1976) was the high tide mark of this asymmetrical philosophy"; "Society was supposed to explain Nature!" (p. 278 as cited by Bloor); §3: the "intermediary solution —social realism alternating with natural relativism— advocated for many years by colleagues like David Bloor or Harry Collins" is "in the long run, counterproductive for the field as well as for their own program". Callon and Latour (1992): "We have never been interested in giving a social explanation of anything, but we want to explain society" (p. 348); their yardstick lets them "read most of SSK as 'reactionary,' because they start from a closed definition of the social and then use this repertoire as an explanation of nature" (p. 349); Collins "simply shifts the burden to the Edinburgh school" (p. 355), though "We learned a great deal from Collins's work" (p. 344). We Have Never Been Modern (1993, p. 94; OCR gaps): Bloor's principle of symmetry "leads rapidly to an impasse"; "Constructivist where Nature is concerned, it is realistic about [Society]". "For David Bloor… and Beyond" (1999): "The Strong Program was useful and still is against the few remaining epistemologists. It has become an obstacle for the continuation of science studies" (p. 116). Bloor's reply: Latour's "criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects" (Anti-Latour, 1999, p. 82); see ssk → latour. Callon has no entry and sits on the sts roster.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: symmetry_dispute holds Bloor and Latour and their 1999 exchange; this arrow extends it back to 1992.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bloor answers that Latour misrepresents the Strong Program and that his own alternative is "obscurantism" (1999); Collins and Yearley had called the actor-network approach a "backward step" (1992)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bloor's own words, read in "Anti-Latour" (SHPS 30, 1999): "Bruno Latour is a vehement critic of the sociology of knowledge in general, and the Strong Program in particular" (p. 81); "I think Latour is wrong ... If anything they are a step backwards" (p. 82); "his criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects, and ... his own approach, in so far as it is different, is unworkable" (p. 82); the charge that SSK explains nature by society "is a profound misrepresentation. The aim isn't to explain nature, but to explain shared beliefs about nature" (p. 87); Latour's vocabulary of actants "looks like a formula for imposing confusion on ourselves: it is obscurantism raised to the level of a general methodological principle" (p. 97); "Latour has endorsed, and encouraged, a wholly false stereotype of the Strong Program", joining "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" (pp. 110–111). He partly concedes: "Latour, rightly, rejects the symmetry principle understood in this way" (p. 84). He cites other critiques he finds "devastating" (p. 95), including Collins and Yearley (1992), Schaffer (1991) and Shapin (1988), none read here. Collins and Yearley's chapter is known only through Callon and Latour's quotations (1992, p. 347): "The consequences of the semiotic method [of Latour] amount to a backward step". Latour's reply acknowledges the charge: "The result is a devastating critique" (1999, p. 113) and calls Schaffer's similar critique "exactly as ill-conceived" (n. 6). Bloor's rejoinder (SHPS 30, pp. 131–136) was not located.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The target is a person entry. On the source side the arrow corresponds to ssk/symmetry_dispute.

proposed_edges.relationship: Kuhn calls the strong programme's claims "absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad" (1991)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kuhn's own words, read: "The Trouble with the Historical Philosophy of Science" (Rothschild Lecture, Harvard, 19 November 1991; published 1992; in The Road Since Structure, 2000): "I am among those who have found the claims of the strong program absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad. And the more qualified sociological and historical formulations that currently strive to replace it are, in my view, scarcely more satisfactory" (p. 110); the strong program "has been widely understood as claiming that power and interest are all there are" (p. 110). In the 1995 Athens interview (same volume) he says of Shapin and Schaffer's Leviathan and the Air-Pump, "The scholarship is often damn good!", while objecting that they "totally miss" the barometer's "vastly greater explanatory power" (pp. 316–317); that remark concerns the science roster's practice strand and is context only. No SSK reply to the lecture was read. The SSK reading of Kuhn ran the other way, as appropriation (Barnes, T. S. Kuhn and Social Science, 1982, unread); edge_132 (kuhn → ssk, influence) stays.

proposed_edges.relationship: A historian of consumption and material culture criticises actor-network theory's "flat view of modern history" while proposing to historicise its concerns (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. Frank Trentmann, "Materiality in the Future of History" (Journal of British Studies 48, 2009; read in full). He writes as a historian of consumption (author note: director of the Cultures of Consumption research programme, 2002–07) and sets material-culture studies against material politics (p. 285). "The most influential (if controversial) platform for exploring the 'agency' of things in the past couple of decades has been actor-network theory (ANT). Spearheaded by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, John Law, and others" (p. 290); n. 33 notes "the difficulty of integrating historical formations of power and culture in an analysis primarily concerned with reconstructing a network of actors and actants at a specific moment in time" (p. 290). "It is perhaps ironic that a theory like ANT, so concerned with resisting grand narratives and abstractions (like 'society'), draws on such a flat view of modern history"; "It is hard to see a general turning away from things, as presumed by Latour and others" (p. 291); "this rather monochromatic view of modernity supposedly so divorced from things" (p. 301). The critique is qualified: "Before simply rejecting Latour as problematic history, however, we might historicize his concerns into questions for research" (p. 301), and whatever one thinks of the claim that things have agency, "things and humans are inseparably interwoven in mutually constitutive relationships" (p. 307). No reply by Latour was found. A historian's critique of Latour; not a claim that consumption history as a field rejected ANT.

proposed.relationship: offers a comparison between programme-based sociological explanation and laboratory ethnography
proposed.evidence_note: Comparative teaching link between two methods, not an assertion of a one-way genealogy or of agreement: the Strong Programme's causal and symmetrical explanation of accepted and rejected belief, and Latour and Woolgar's laboratory ethnography of how facts are made. Shared objects do not establish a simple Bloor-to-Latour lineage. The acknowledged debt is edge_685. The disagreement of 1992–99 is carried by the two critique edges of revision 1.135 (latour → ssk and ssk → latour), which hold the Bloor–Latour exchange and its sources.

row.context: A historian of science at the 1965 symposium on Kuhn, sceptical of Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time" (1970, p. 50). He kept using both as guides; Kuhn replied that he dissented "from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws".
row.works: "Normal Science, Scientific Revolutions and the History of Science" (1970)

row.context: A historian of consumption who calls for a history of materiality joining material culture to politics and practice; he questions actor-network theory's "flat view of modern history" while proposing to "historicize" Latour's concerns (2009).
row.works: "Materiality in the Future of History: Things, Practices, and Politics" (2009)
